arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Ms. Bell argued the statute requires intent to defraud a financial institution.
Mr. Yang argued the required intent is to deceive the bank to deprive it of value.
Chief Justice Roberts noted that insurance rates rise when property is stolen repeatedly.
Justice Ginsburg asked if Shaw could be convicted under a different statutory clause.

case.dek: The dispute centers on whether a defendant must intend to deprive a bank of its own assets or if intent to harm a customer's property suffices.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: Shaw stole a customer's car from a bank lot. The government charged him with defrauding the bank. Shaw argues the bank suffered no direct loss. The government argues the bank's interest was harmed.

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The Supreme Court heard oral argument in this case on October 4, 2016.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Shaw wants the conviction overturned because he did not intend to harm the bank's own property.
The government wants the conviction upheld because Shaw intended to harm the bank's possessory interest.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Shaw argues the statute requires intent to deprive the bank of its own value.
The government argues the statute covers intent to harm any interest the bank holds.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Kennedy asked if the intent targets whoever holds a lawful possessory interest.
Justice Breyer asked if theft is impossible when the defendant believes the property is insured.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the scope of federal bank fraud laws. It determines whether prosecutors can charge theft of customer property as a crime against the bank. The outcome shapes how courts interpret financial institution protections.
